primary.text: Then one AI made its own obstacle course. It placed eight blocks around a building called the cathedral. Then it jumped across without touching the ground. It made the course and its rules all by itself. It kept itself busy, though nobody had asked it to. The researchers say this is a feature of play.
primary.label: NUMERIC_EQUIVALENCE_MATCH

primary.text: But the jumps were not the only thing to watch. In the test, the island and conversation reset every hour, but the work area with the AI's notes and programs carried over to the next hour. The island went back to how it was before, but the AI's discoveries stayed.
primary.label: NORMALIZED_MATCH

primary.text: So would this experience help the AI when it was asked to work again? The researchers compared 13 AIs with island experience. They also used 13 AIs with the same setup, but no experience. On a new island, the task was to build as many towers as possible in one hour. Each tower had to be five blocks high. The researchers checked which AIs could build more than two towers. The experienced group did better. Those that had taken a detour were now one step ahead.
primary.label: NORMALIZED_MATCH

primary.text: The researchers also erased a way to throw rocks to get more blocks from one AI's memory. After that, the average number of towers it could build went down. Its scores on other tasks stayed the same. For this AI, at least, remembering that way helped it build towers. One tip in the strategy notes was worth paying attention to.
primary.label: NUMERIC_EQUIVALENCE_MATCH

primary.text: Even so, it is too soon to wave a flag and say play and get smarter proves complete. The experienced group did better, and removing one memory lowered its score. These two results need to be studied separately. By themselves, they do not show that play itself made a difference.
primary.label: TRUE_CONTENT_MISMATCH
